articles.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
articles.summary: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

top_comments: While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now. Following a few bugs and bad proofs this year, there are a number of different implementations, in different languages, and with different levels of proofs of their consistency. con-leche and con-ron are the heavy hitters, with consistency proofs of themselves. So for RH to be false, there'd have to be a bug in all the kernels that affects both the consistency proofs and the RH proof itself.
If I understand correctly, for the purpose of the proof Claude formalized a huge chunk of all modern math. So it's a big result not only for GRH, but math foundations and formalization.

A fake refutation of the Collatz conjecture already got through one of these independent checkers in the past.What's harder, proving GRH or finding a way to get through every checker (which aren't as independent as they are sometimes touted to be)?In this case there was a human expert in the loop so it's much less likely the model hacked its way through the problem without the expert noticing. But the statement as written has 4 points, none of which rests on the human involvement. So I don't like that they claim full confidence based on those points.

articles.title: Detonating a pile of lead azide
articles.summary: Detonating a pile of lead azide

top_comments: Have worked with primary explosives like lead azide. Blame and criminal liability should be allocated to the idiots who allowed an enormous amount to sit uninspected for 20 years.Degraded primaries (dried, recrystallized - so many ways to be super-sensitized) can detonate in response to a loud noise. Forget sending in robotics to move drums of this anywhere. An effector touching a drum can cause container flexure sufficient to detonate the material.This is a horrific hazmat problem. There's no safe solution, only those with lower probability of bad outcomes. I wish them well.

For everyone suggesting robots can move it:If you work in a lab that handles chemicals that can explode like this (organic peroxides, etc.) and you find something in a state like this, the proper response is literally to have the bomb squad come out and destroy your 1L or whatever of material in place. They literally can not shift these barrels without the entire thing detonating.

That's how a lot in our modern society operates. Hide the problem until it's impossible to hide, then when it's so bad there are no good solutions left, block any viable solution with at least manageable fallout because it's "unsafe" and wait until it blows up randomly. And everybody feels they've done their best, and nobody suffers any consequences for the screwup except for innocent bystanders.

articles.title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
articles.summary: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

top_comments: This reminds me of a (completely different, but felt equally) bizzare problem with ghostty (the terminal emulator) on Linux and Steam, specifically Baldur's Gate 3.At the start of the game after an update, BG3 compiles the (Vulkan) shaders. To avoid hammering the computer, it checks the load, including I/O pressure, and then throttles itself. It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if it's not doing anything this somehow counts as pressure. This was made worse by the fact that I usually have a dozen or so Ghostty windows.End result, BG3 compiles shaders using 1 core, throttled, instead of all available 20 cores. Instead of a minute or so, it'd take several hours.(For closure: I configured ghostty to use epoll instead. Probably not optimal but works around the problem.)
Better description: "My USB network switch was cutting my download speed".The fact that it's a monitor is a little bit irrelevant.

Since lots of comments misunderstood the article, the extra latency from going through the monitor meant his laptop couldn't acknowledge the packets quickly enough. That led a buffer on the ethernet adapter to fill and that led it to drop packets.A different adapter which required less frequent acknowledgement fixed the problem for him.It is quite a nice post which gets to the bottom of incredibly opaque behaviour of USB hubs.

If you're new to quantized models: Don't get too excited about claims of fitting large models into tiny RAM footprints from random GitHub repos. There is always a tradeoff, and it's too easy to benchmaxx KL-divergence numbers and even single benchmark scores. Just because you can get something to run on a device doesn't mean it's going to be useful. The headline claim of this repo (12X better) doesn't even apply to Inkling-2-MiniThis repo's README is a mess of different histories as the author bounces from one popular model to the next. It refers to vague things like "the 1.2GB file" that probably made sense in an early vibecoding pass, but are now lost after the repo has been pushed around to different popular models.The truth is that random GitHub repos with messy READMEs almost never hold a real secret that the mainstream quantizations have missed. I would recommend sticking to mainstream quantizations like the official GGML release, Unsloth's quants, or the more well known community quantizers like bartowski or AesSedai. They typically follow an optimized size-quality tradeoff so you can find the one that fits your needs.When you see a repo like this where everything is so obviously vibecoded that the README is a rambling mix of projects and claims, you should probably go looking for a more authoritative source. The local LLM communities get spammed with 10 of these types of projects per day but I have yet to see a real breakthrough come from any of the vibecoded ones. The real work is coming from people who study this and have compute to test at scale or work on implementing advanced techniques which require inference engine support, like trellis quants.
Our future hinges on the capability gap between frontier lab models and open source local models

I had a rough time with llama.cpp so fixed the bugs in it for performance some notes you need a minimum of 12gb of vram for credible performance with decent context length above 100k...The best I could do with established techniques and staying at nvfp4 levels of quant, is around 40-45 toks/s on 5070 Ti with 800 toks/s prefill around 128k kv cache... with the kernels matching output byte for byte and basic manual verification of the patched code.3060 sits around 20-25 toks/s with prefill around 350-400 toks/s i think maybe it can be improved but my 3060 system was ddr4 so not the greatest.Either way at below 6gb you cant run beyond q4 quants at above 10-20 tok/s with pretty small context size, afaik that gets awfully close to the roofline depending on expert cache hit rate... unless you quant the logits into the ground.

articles.title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
articles.summary: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

top_comments: I am constantly surprised how few mentions of Slint there are in these sorts of articles. It's written by a team of funded ex-Qt alumni, is incredibly fast, and their DSL approach, while having a bit of a learning curve, makes laying out apps and managing data binding incredibly easy.They also bypass a big part of the issues mentioned in the article by just straight up using skia as a renderer on desktop (you can use others if you want) which gives software and gpu accelerated paths.I'm not associated with the project at all, but have been using it on and off for a couple years and have been quite satisfied.It's main weakness is rich text rendering which lacks maturity for complex layouts, but it is getting better all the time.

The "2026 Survey of Rust GUI Libraries" does not include Native Shell (nsh) [1] which is retained-mode and based on gpui-fast.Maybe because the code repository was started on October 11th, just 1.5 months ago. More than 2,000 commits later it already looks great. I think, they do the (AI) software engineering part very well [2].After using GTK and JavaFX, and React for a decade, Native Shell makes me really excited. I never got warm with Flutter, the desktop applications were very slow on my MacBook. So I've been doing frontend development for more than 25 years, and I'm completely mind-blown for the last few weeks.Having a React background this feels very familiar, without the annoyances. Reactivity is inspired by Solid, styling by CSS (optionally with Tailwind syntax), the UI primitives are native views with layouting done by Taffy [3]. If you target web, the UI will be HTML. You can write the UI screens and components in Rust, but you can also use TypeScript/JSX, it will transpile and interpret it using Rolldown and QuickJS.It includes some components which are difficult to get right. A data table component, a rich-text editor component, and a plot component. As far as I can tell, they chose the currently best-known approach for them.[1] https://nsh.dev/ [2] https://github.com/longbridge/nsh/commits/main [3] https://nsh.dev/elements/

I'm building a custom GUI in Rust and it is such a slow process to build out. I find bits of the end result to be amazing, but it's all in the details that look like nothing compared to using something more "complete" with a larger UI community.I have some nice markdown rendering and phenomenally fast smooth scrolling - but I look at everything ahead of me, I don't even have text selection implemented yet, text wrapping and input cursor placement implementation wasn't that smooth to begin with. I have some amazing shader based animations, but the amount of effort that went into far exceed anything else I could have picked for a foundation.I started with Typescript and kept running into performance issues - it was fast to build and easy to scale, but kept becoming harder to maintain. With Rust it feels hard to build, hard to scale, but it feels like scaling and maintaining might be starting to get easier. The performance ceiling is a night a day difference though.
